To temporize means to deliberately delay taking a clear position or making a definite decision — not out of confusion, but as a calculated tactic to buy yourself more time.

When someone temporizes, they are stalling on purpose. They avoid giving a direct answer, avoid committing to a course of action, and avoid showing their hand — all while keeping things moving just enough so that nobody notices they're not actually deciding anything.

The key word here is deliberate. A person who temporizes isn't lost or genuinely unsure. They know they're stalling. They're doing it strategically, usually because the timing isn't right for them to reveal their true position, or because they're hoping the situation will change in their favor if they just wait long enough.
What it looks like in real life

Imagine a manager asks an employee, "Do you support the new company policy?" The employee personally dislikes it but doesn't want to say so openly — not yet. So instead of answering, they say, "That's an important question. I'd like to review the details more carefully before giving you a complete answer." The manager asks again a week later, and the employee says, "I'm still evaluating all the implications." This person is temporizing — they're giving just enough of a response to satisfy the moment without actually committing to anything.

Now imagine a country at war. A general knows he needs reinforcements before he can attack, but the enemy is pushing for a battle now. So he sends back long, complicated messages, raises small diplomatic concerns, asks for clarification on things that don't need clarification — all to stretch the clock without openly refusing to fight. That is also temporizing.

A politician who keeps saying "I believe we need to look at this issue from all angles" every time they're asked directly about their stance on a bill is temporizing. A business executive who responds to a merger offer with "We appreciate the proposal and will be conducting a thorough internal review" — while quietly hoping a better offer comes along — is temporizing.
The full range of the word

Temporizing can happen in a few slightly different ways, all connected by the same thread:

The first is verbal evasion — giving vague, non-committal, or deliberately ambiguous answers to avoid locking yourself into a position. This is the most common use. The person speaks, but says nothing that pins them down.

The second is going along temporarily — agreeing with or adapting to the current situation not because you believe in it, but just to avoid conflict or confrontation right now, while you wait for a better moment to push back. You don't fight the tide; you float with it for a while.

The third is buying time through minor actions — doing just enough to appear engaged while the real decision keeps getting pushed further into the future. Asking for more data, calling extra meetings, requesting additional review — when the real purpose is delay, not discovery.

Temporizing usually carries a slightly negative or at least suspicious connotation. When we say someone is temporizing, we're often suggesting that they're being evasive, cowardly, or self-serving — that they're avoiding the discomfort of a real decision at someone else's expense, or that they're being strategically dishonest by pretending to engage while actually doing nothing.

That said, temporizing isn't always morally wrong. Sometimes it's wise and even necessary. A diplomat who temporizes during a tense negotiation to prevent a rash decision from both sides may be doing exactly the right thing. A doctor who gives a cautious, non-committal answer while waiting for test results rather than alarming a patient prematurely is also temporizing in a responsible way. Context determines whether it's shrewd or spineless.
How it differs from similar words

Procrastinate means to delay something due to laziness, anxiety, or avoidance of discomfort — it's more about weakness than strategy. Temporizing is calculated; procrastinating is usually not.

Equivocate means to use deliberately unclear or ambiguous language — often to deceive or mislead. Equivocation is about the words you use. Temporizing is broader — it's about the behavior of stalling, which may or may not involve equivocation.

Stall is the closest everyday synonym. Temporizing is essentially a more formal and precise word for stalling, with an added sense of doing so diplomatically or politically, rather than just bluntly dragging your feet.

Vacillate means to go back and forth between two positions out of genuine indecision. A person who vacillates actually can't make up their mind. A person who temporizes may know exactly what they think — they're just not ready to say it yet.

Hedge means to avoid taking a firm stance in order to protect yourself from being wrong. Hedging is about keeping options open; temporizing is specifically about stretching time.
The situations where it most commonly appears

You'll encounter this word most often in political, diplomatic, military, legal, and business contexts — anywhere that decisions carry high stakes and where delay can itself be a form of power. Leaders temporize during crises. Negotiators temporize at the table. Executives temporize with boards. Generals temporize with enemies. It's a word built for situations where time is a resource, and someone is deliberately spending it.
One-sentence summary to lock it in
To temporize is to deliberately stall — giving vague or non-committal responses and avoiding any firm decision — as a strategic way to gain more time before you have to show your hand.
